claims.text: NbTi + AlCrMo forms protective Cr2O3 and CrNbO4 oxide layers during high-temperature oxidation.
The protective Cr-rich oxide layer impedes inward oxygen diffusion.
Protective oxide formation is the key mechanism responsible for the high-temperature oxidation resistance of NbTi + AlCrMo.
Protective oxide formation enables the alloy to have low density.
Protective oxide formation enables the alloy to retain mechanical strength.
Protective oxide formation enables corrosion resistance distinct from high-temperature oxidation resistance.
NbTi + AlCrMo is a lightweight alloy with a density of 7.2 g/cm3.
NbTi + AlCrMo is a refractory medium-entropy alloy.
Increasing Cr content promotes formation of protective CrNbO4 and Cr2O3 oxides and improves oxidation resistance.
Mo addition causes the formation of the protective Cr2O3 and CrNbO4 oxides.
Mo may benefit oxidation resistance because of its low oxygen solubility while protective Cr-rich layers are present.
The proposed mechanism operates under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
NbTi + AlCrMo exhibits improved oxidation resistance relative to an NbTi alloy containing neither Cr nor Mo.
The mechanism should cease to hold at extreme temperatures or in environments that disrupt protective-oxide formation.
Composition affects the formation and continuity of protective oxide layers.
Processing conditions affect formation of the protective oxide layers.
Tensile and oxidation tests across varying Cr and Mo contents are proposed as the experimental test.
A lack of correlation between protective-oxide formation and enhanced oxidation resistance and low density would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated initial material is already NbTi + AlCrMo and therefore already contains Cr and Mo, while the intervention is described as adding Cr and Mo. It is unclear whether the intervention starts from NbTi or modifies an already Cr/Mo-containing alloy.
The baseline is NbTi without Cr and Mo, but the proposed modified material also contains Al; consequently, the comparison does not isolate the effects of Cr and Mo.
The falsification rule depends on protective-oxide formation and density, but the listed measurements include neither oxide-layer characterization nor density.

The broad hypothesis claims corrosion resistance and mechanical strength, but the predicted outcome omits corrosion and gives no directional strength prediction; the experiment therefore cannot decisively test the full claimed property combination.
